title: Multi-Tenant Architecture
summary: Multi-tenancy trades isolation for efficiency. Choose among silo, bridge, and pool models for compute and data — and make noisy-neighbor, blast radius, and encryption boundaries explicit.

sections.title: Isolation spectrum
paragraphs: Silo: dedicated resources per tenant (strong isolation, high cost). Pool: shared everything with logical separation (efficient, riskier). Bridge models mix — e.g., shared app tier, separate DB schemas/clusters for large tenants.
The right point on the spectrum depends on threat model, compliance, and tenant size skew.

sections.title: Data plane concerns
paragraphs: Row-level tenancy needs ruthless discipline on every query (tenant_id predicates, RLS). Schema-per-tenant eases isolation but complicates migrations. Database-per-tenant maximizes isolation and operational load.
Encryption keys per tenant, backup isolation, and restore procedures are part of the design — not afterthoughts.

sections.title: Control plane and noisy neighbors
paragraphs: Fair scheduling, per-tenant rate limits, and quotas prevent one tenant from exhausting shared pools. Load shedding should be tenant-aware.
Observability must tag every metric/log/trace with tenant for cost attribution and incident scoping.

sections.title: Migration between models
paragraphs: Plan how a growing tenant graduates from pool to silo without downtime. Many outages happen during 'VIP tenant' exceptionalism without automation.

deepDive.title: Multi-Tenant Architecture — Operations
paragraphs: Operating Multi-Tenant Architecture in production means defining SLIs before tuning knobs, knowing amplification costs, and rehearsing failure modes.
Prefer reversible changes, feature flags, and canaries. Measure p50/p99 and error rate under load that matches production skew.
bullets: Define capacity from the scarcest resource
Keep rollback cheaper than forward repair when possible

deepDive.title: Multi-Tenant Architecture — Failure modes
paragraphs: Common failures around Multi-Tenant Architecture include overload, partial dependency outages, and silent correctness bugs that pass happy-path tests.
Inject faults in staging: latency, loss, clock skew, and disk full. Verify alerts fire and degradation is intentional.

expert.title: Multi-Tenant Architecture — Expert notes
paragraphs: At the expert level, Multi-Tenant Architecture intersects multi-region consistency, cost envelopes, and organizational constraints (team ownership, on-call load).
Write down the non-goals. Many outages come from optimizing a metric that was never the product requirement.

practices: Default-deny data access with tenant context
pitfalls: Missing tenant filters on a single query path
One giant tenant without isolation plan
keyTakeaways: Every layer must enforce tenant context
whyItMatters: Most SaaS products are multi-tenant. Weak tenancy design causes security incidents and chronic performance pain.
reflectionQuestions: Where could a missing tenant predicate leak data in your stack?
numbersToKnow: Know your p99 latency budget before adding hops
Peak load ≠ average load — plan headroom (often 2–3×)
Cross-region RTT is often ~50–150ms one way
